Since $(1-|z|)/|1-z| \asymp 1$ nontangentially at $z=1$ and $\to 0$ at other points, we need $|\phi(z)| \to 0$ nontangentially at $z=1$ and $|\phi(z)| \cdot ((1-|z|)/|1-z|)^p \to 0$ at other points (which is automatic if $\phi$ doesn't grow too fast).

So we need an analytic function $\phi$ with:
- $|\phi(z)| \to 0$ nontangentially at $z=1$
- $\sup_\theta |\phi(re^{i\theta})| \cdot ((1-r)/|1-re^{i\theta}|)^p \not\to 0$

The second condition means there's a sequence $r_n, \theta_n$ with $|\phi(r_n e^{i\theta_n})| \cdot ((1-r_n)/|1-r_n e^{i\theta_n}|)^p \geq \epsilon$.

If $\theta_n \not\to 0$, then $|1-r_n e^{i\theta_n}| \to |1-e^{i\theta_n}| > 0$ (assuming $\theta_n$ has a limit $\neq 0$), so $((1-r_n)/|1-r_n e^{i\theta_n}|)^p \to 0$, and we'd need $|\phi(r_n e^{i\theta_n})| \to \infty$, which means $\phi$ is unbounded. But then we also need $|\phi(z)| \to 0$ nontangentially at $z=1$.

If $\theta_n \to 0$ but tangentially (i.e., $\theta_n / (1-r_n) \to \infty$), then $|1-r_n e^{i\theta_n}| \approx |\theta_n| \gg (1-r_n)$, so $((1-r_n)/|1-r_n e^{i\theta_n}|)^p \approx ((1-r_n)/\theta_n)^p \to 0$. So we'd need $|\phi(r_n e^{i\theta_n})| \gg ((\theta_n)/(1-r_n))^p \to \infty$.

So $\phi$ needs to grow along a tangential sequence near $z=1$, while decaying nontangentially at $z=1$.
